Title: Guidelines for Charitable Organisations on Fundraising from the Public
URL: https://www.fssu.ie/app/uploads/2024/05/charities-regulator-guidance-for-fundraising-english.pdf
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
These Guidelines are issued by the Charities Regulator pursuant to section 14(1) (i) of the Charities Act 2009, to encourage and facilitate the better administration and management of charitable organisations (charities).
...
The Charities Regulator was established in October 2014 as Ireland’s statutory 
independent authority for the regulation and protection of charitable trusts and 
organisations (charities). Under the Charities Act 2009, the Charities Regulator’s 
general functions are to: 
increase public trust and confidence in the management and administration of 
charitable trusts and charitable organisations; 
promote compliance by charity trustees with their duties in the control and 
management of charitable trusts and charitable organisations; 
promote the effective use of the property of charitable trusts or charitable 
organisations; 
ensure the accountability of charitable organisations to donors and beneficiaries of 
charitable gifts, and the public; 
promote understanding of the requirement that charitable purposes confer a public 
benefit; 
establish and maintain a register of charitable organisations; 
ensure and monitor compliance by charitable organisations with this Act; 
carry out investigations in accordance with this Act; 
encourage and facilitate the better administration and management of charitable 
organisations by the provision of information or advice, including in particular by way 
of issuing (or, as it considers appropriate, approving) guidelines, codes of conduct, and 
model constitutional documents; 
carry on such activities or publish such information (including statistical information) 
concerning charitable organisations and charitable trusts as it considers appropriate; 
provide information (including statistical information) or advice, or make proposals, to 
the Minister on matters relating to the functions of the Regulator.
...
However, it is critical that charities carry out all fundraising from the public in an open, transparent, honest, respectful and accountable manner. Fundraising should always be underpinned by an appropriate legal framework. Fundraising activities which operate on the basis of perceived loopholes in the law risk damaging the reputation of the charity and the sector more generally. The basis for these Guidelines is the 2008 Statement of Guiding Principles on Charitable Fundraising. These Guidelines have benefitted from the input of a Consultative Panel on Charitable Fundraising which was set up by the Charities Regulator in 2016 at the request of the Minister for Justice and Equality. They have also been informed by evidence-based research and a public consultation which took place in Autumn 2016. The Charities Regulator expects that any charities that fundraise will do so in a way which protects the reputations of their charity and encourages public trust and confidence in their charity and in charities more generally. This includes following the law and recognised standards, protecting the charity from undue risk and showing respect for beneficiaries, donors and the public. These Guidelines are intended to assist trustees of a charity to run the charity effectively, avoid difficulties in respect of fundraising activities and comply with their legal duties. Charities vary in terms of their size and activities. Trustees should consider and decide how best to apply these Guidelines to their charity’s particular circumstances. The Charities Regulator requires the trustees of each registered Irish charity to be able to explain and justify their approach to fundraising from the public, particularly if they decide not to follow good practice as set out in these Guidelines.
...
These Guidelines apply to all types of fundraising from the public for the benefit of charities and their beneficiaries. It applies whether or not: fundraising from the public is a small or major part of the charity’s approach to raising money, or; fundraising is carried out by the charity, by a subsidiary trading company on behalf of the charity, by another person or organisation on the charity’s behalf or by a person or organisation who uses the charity’s name in advertising. Trustees should ensure that all key people within their charity who are involved in fundraising implement the approaches and practices set out in these Guidelines. These include senior management, staff, company directors, volunteers and any professional fundraisers. Donors, potential donors and members of the public can also use the Guidelines to ensure they are educated and informed prior to making a donation.
...
Trustees should be assured that any donations sought indirectly, such as through third party agents, are solicited and received in full conformity with the law, the charity’s own fundraising policies and procedures and these Guidelines. Fundraising by third party agents should be the subject of a written contract. Trustees should ensure the contract is clear and specific as to the cost of the fundraising, including the percentage of each charitable donation that will go to the charitable purpose. Donors have a right to expect that their gift is being used primarily for the charitable purpose. A charity must not enter into any agreement which is intended to deliver more private benefit to third party fundraisers than it does to the charity.
...
; 10
...
All personal data must be collected fairly and lawfully and information which can be identified or attributed to one or more individuals must be treated as confidential. A charity must comply with all legal requirements with regard to data protection legislation. The Charities Regulator also expects charities to conform to relevant guidance issued by the Data Protection Commissioner, in particular, the Data Protection in the Charity and Voluntary Sector Guidelines 2 as well as guidance relating to direct and inter-active marketing, including direct mail, email, telemarketing, digital and social media marketing, SMS text etc. A charity should respect donors’ stated preferences regarding contact by the charity and should make it easy to communicate these preferences. Where a third party firm or agent is employed by a charity to fundraise, the public have a right to reasonably assume that any data they provide is held only by the charity and not by the third party.
...
Trustees must ensure the following: The charity keeps proper books of account, which correctly record and explain transactions; Internal financial control procedures are in place to ensure that funds are used effectively and to minimise the risk of funds being misused; The charity reports annually to the Charities Regulator. Charities should be in a position to provide a full financial account of each individual fundraising event. This includes the gross amount of funds raised, the associated fundraising costs and to which charitable purpose or charitable fund the proceeds of the event have been allocated. The Charities Regulator has published separate Guidelines on Internal Financial Controls for charities (available on our website). The Guidelines give practical guidance in relation to the main areas of financial control for charities: income; expenditure; banking (including payments and loans); assets and investments and monitoring arrangements. They contain a number of useful checklists for charities to ensure they have the appropriate controls in place. Charities are expected to follow the good practice set out in these Guidelines.
...
Their primary aim is to encourage and facilitate the better administration and management of charity fundraising from the public. The Charities Regulator’s monitoring approach is primarily informed by the provisions of the Charities Act 2009. These provisions place specific and general duties on each charity and its charity trustees. They also provide the Charities Regulator with powers to register, monitor, investigate and sanction charities, as appropriate.

Title: Charitable Solicitation Laws, Requirements, and Penalties - LegalClarity
URL: https://legalclarity.org/charitable-solicitation-laws-requirements-and-penalties/
Published: 2026-05-14T05:35:47.000Z
Author: N/A
Highlights:
Before soliciting donations, most nonprofits must register with the state — and the rules get more complex when fundraising online or across state lines.
...
Roughly 39 states and the District of Columbia require charitable organizations to register with a state agency before asking residents for donations, and each state sets its own rules, fees, and exemptions. If your nonprofit raises money in more than one state, you likely need separate registrations in each one. Failing to register can trigger fines, fundraising bans, and even criminal charges in some jurisdictions. The registration process itself is manageable once you know what documents to gather and where to file, but the real complexity comes from keeping up with annual renewals and understanding which rules apply when your fundraising crosses state lines.
...
Religious organizations are the most universally exempted category. Most states with registration requirements exempt churches, mosques, synagogues, and other houses of worship, though the scope of the exemption varies. Some states exempt only the congregation itself, while others extend the exemption to religiously affiliated charities that derive most of their funding from the parent denomination. Educational institutions with accredited curricula and enrolled student bodies also frequently qualify for exemptions.
...
A website with a “Donate Now” button can theoretically reach donors in every state, and that raises the question of whether you need to register everywhere. The most widely referenced guidance comes from the Charleston Principles, developed by the National Association of State Charity Officials. The core idea: simply having a website that accepts donations does not automatically require registration in every state. But if you actively target a specific state’s residents through advertising, email campaigns, or social media outreach, or if you receive repeated and substantial donations from a particular state, you’ve likely crossed the line into solicitation there.
...
In practice, this puts many smaller nonprofits in an uncomfortable position. Strict compliance would mean registering in all 39-plus jurisdictions that require it, which is expensive and administratively heavy. Many organizations take a risk-based approach: they register in their home state and in any state where they actively market, hold events, or have a significant donor base, and they accept the low-probability risk of enforcement in states where their connection is passive. Larger nonprofits with national fundraising programs usually register across the board.
...
Virtual fundraising events add another layer. Online auctions, raffles, and charitable gaming streams may trigger not just solicitation registration but separate charitable gaming permits, depending on the state. If you’re planning a virtual gala with a nationwide audience, treat it like a multi-state solicitation and register accordingly rather than hoping nobody notices.
...
To reduce duplication, the Unified Registration Statement consolidates the information most states need into a single standardized form. It’s accepted by 36 states and the District of Columbia, though some of those jurisdictions also require supplemental state-specific forms. The URS covers basics like your legal name, federal employer identification number, contact information, and fundraising methods. You still submit a separate copy to each state, but at least the core document is the same.
...
A related initiative, the Multistate
...
system. As of early 2025, though, only two states participate, so it’s not yet a practical substitute for individual
...
jurisdictions that require
...
filings. The typical fee falls between $25 and $300
...
with many states clustering around the $25 to $50 range. Some states use sliding scales tied to your total revenue or contributions, so larger organizations pay more. A handful of states charge no fee at all for
...
initial registration but impose fees
...
annual renewals. Before you budget, check each target state’s fee schedule on the attorney general’
...
or secretary of state’s website, because these amounts change periodically.
...
Most registrations go to the state attorney general’s office, though some states assign oversight to the secretary of state or a dedicated charities bureau. Check the specific agency for each state before mailing anything to the wrong place. Many states now accept electronic filings through their own online portals, and a growing number accept scanned documents uploaded through those systems. For states that still require paper filings, send your packet by certified mail so you have proof of submission.
...
Registration is not a one-time event. Every state with a registration requirement also requires periodic renewals, almost always annually. The renewal filing typically includes an updated IRS Form 990 and current financial statements. Most states set the renewal deadline relative to the close of your fiscal year, commonly four and a half to six months after year-end, which aligns with the Form 990 due date.
...
Missing a renewal deadline is where things get expensive and disruptive. Late fees typically start at $25 per month and can escalate significantly in states with aggressive enforcement. More importantly, some states automatically suspend your right to solicit donations once your registration lapses, meaning every dollar you raise while unregistered is potentially unlawful. Reinstating a lapsed registration often requires paying all accumulated late fees, filing all overdue reports, and sometimes paying a separate re-registration fee.
...
State attorneys general take unauthorized solicitation seriously, and the consequences go well beyond a fine in the mail. Enforcement tools include:
...
into compliance.
...
- Civil penalties: Fines vary widely. Some states assess penalties per violation, meaning each solicitation sent without registration counts separately. Fines of $1,000 to $5,000 per violation are common in states with aggressive enforcement.
...
- Criminal charges: In some states, soliciting without registration or filing false information can be charged as a misdemeanor or even a felony for repeat offenders.
...
The practical risk is highest for organizations that solicit aggressively in a state without registering. A quiet website that happens to accept a donation from a state where you’re not registered is unlikely to draw attention. But running a direct mail campaign, buying advertising, or hiring a solicitor to make calls into a state where you’re unregistered is the kind of activity that triggers enforcement. Attorneys general often discover violations through donor complaints, so treating donors well is both good ethics and good compliance strategy.
...
A professional solicitor is someone who, for compensation, directly asks the public for donations on behalf of a charity. This is the more heavily regulated category. In most states, professional solicitors must register independently with the state before conducting any fundraising, and the registration requirements are substantially more burdensome than what the charity itself faces. Registration fees for solicitors can range up to $1,000, and roughly 38 states also require solicitors to post a surety bond. Bond amounts vary by state, with figures typically ranging from a few thousand dollars up to $50,000.
...
written contract between the charity and the solicitor must be in place before
...
that contract to be filed with the regulating agency. The contract must spell out the percentage of funds the solicitor retains, the duration of the arrangement, and the methods the solicitor will use. After
...
campaign ends, the solicitor typically must file an accounting of all funds received and distributed. Operating without a license or bond can result in significant fines and, in states with criminal enforcement provisions, fraud charges.

Charitable solicitations registration is a state compliance issue, not federal. Currently, 41 states plus Washington, DC*, require charities to register with the state division of charities prior to soliciting the public for donations. Your particular state’s agency may be called something else, but chances are, your state requires registration. In most states with a mandatory filing requirement, it is the state Attorney General’s office that governs this. In others, it is the Secretary of State’s office. There are even a handful of states, like our home state of Tennessee, where both state agencies have a hand in it.

In many others, is a substantial application, requiring budget projections, the disclosure of board of directors information, and even copies of your IRS Form 990 or 501(c)(3) determination letter. More than half of the states will not allow you to register prior to receiving IRS 501(c)(3) status.

For example, let’s suppose you are a Florida-based charity and you want to begin targeting potential supporters in neighboring Georgia. Even if you are properly registered in Florida, your nonprofit will still have to comply with Georgia’s registration requirements.

The Spam Act 2003 sets out strict rules on when and how you can send commercial electronic messages. If you’re running a business in Australia, understanding these rules isn’t just about avoiding fines - it’s about building trust with your audience and protecting your brand.

Australia has some of the toughest anti‑spam laws in the world. The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) actively monitors compliance and takes enforcement action where needed.
...
The Spam Act covers “commercial electronic messages” sent by email, SMS, MMS or instant messaging. A message is “commercial” if it offers, advertises or promotes goods, services, land, business or investment opportunities - or if it assists in doing so (for example, asking people to visit your online store).

Title: Don’t Filter This Out: Are You Spam Act Compliant? | Global law firm | Norton Rose Fulbright
URL: https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/en/knowledge/publications/5615dd36/dont-filter-this-out-are-you-spam-act-compliant
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
Throughout 2023, the Australian Media and Communications Authority (ACMA) has escalated its enforcement actions for non-compliance with the Spam Act 2003 (Cth) (Spam Act). Consistent with its enforcement priorities for 2023-2024, ACMA has increased surveillance and has issued a record number of fines, including its largest penalty of $3.55 million. Multiple businesses across a variety of sectors have been penalised for Spam Act contraventions, including Ticketek, The Wine Group, Sportsbet, Kogan Australia, Woolworths Group and Uber.
...
The Spam Act governs the sending of promotional messages and material via email and SMS, and, as a consequence, it regulates most aspects of a business’ marketing activity. Now more than ever, Australian businesses need to be aware of their obligations under the Spam Act and ensure their policies and processes for email and SMS marketing are compliant.
...
- The sending of marketing material via SMS, email or instant message to persons (defined in the Spam Act as commercial electronic messages – CEMs) without consent;
- Marketing messages sent without a functional ‘unsubscribe facility.’ A functional unsubscribe facility must state how a person can unsubscribe and must enable them to easily do so by clicking a link or sending a message (e.g. ‘stop’); and
- The sending of marketing messages more than 5 business days after a person has taken steps to unsubscribe.
...
ACMA has broad-ranging enforcement powers under the Spam Act, including issuing infringement notices for pecuniary penalties. Penalties are calculated by reference to the number of messages sent in contravention of the Spam Act per day (see Schedule 3 to the Spam Act).
...
By way of example, a business that sent more than 50 CEMs without consent on one day would be liable for a fine of 1,000 penalty units (currently $313,000 if the contraventions occurred after 1 July 2023). Given the nature of mass marketing, it is not uncommon for businesses to send hundreds or thousands of CEMs each day over many months. Accordingly, the potential penalties may reach to tens of millions and require judicial discretion to reduce the penalty. Most recently, Doordash Technologies Australia received an infringement notice of over $2 million for contraventions occurring across 12 days from July to October 2022.
...
- Failure to have express or inferred consent for the sending of electronic marketing material, and ensuring records of consent are maintained and updated;
- Messages sent for mixed purposes – both informative and commercial;
- Delay in addressing complaints from customers about spam; and
- Reliance on third party marketing companies and SMS providers.
...
Unless an exception applies, consent is required for the sending of CEMs. The Spam Act differentiates between express and inferred consent. Ultimately, the business that sends a CEM bears the onus of establishing consent and should ensure that records are properly maintained and processes are regularly reviewed.
...
For example, businesses should ensure that consent is genuinely obtained (whether expressly through terms accepted by a customer or on the basis of being reasonably inferred), unsubscribe processes operate correctly and records are updated, customer-facing staff are properly trained to obtain and record consent, and sign-up and registration processes are compliant. Businesses may risk contravening the Spam Act if they fail to take these steps.
...
containing only factual information (such as updates on the delivery status of a customer’s order)
...

...
to comply with these requirements
...
Complaints received from customers about spam are often the first indication that a business’ systems of providing electronic marketing material may be non-compliant. It is prudent for businesses to be timely in addressing complaints so as to mitigate the risk of those complaints being escalated to ACMA.
...
If complaints are made to ACMA, ACMA may issue businesses with a Spam Compliance Alert, which provides notice
...
customer complaints. Early engagement and self-reporting to ACMA is advised to minimise the risk of a formal investigation and enforcement action.
...
It is common industry practice for businesses to rely on third party providers to manage customer databases and to send SMS and email messages on their behalf. Businesses must be alive to the fact that compliance with the Spam Act cannot be delegated to third party providers and businesses will remain liable for all CEMs sent to customers, including by third party providers.
...
- Regular reviews of policies and procedures, including a business’ general terms and conditions and privacy policy, as well as processes for obtaining, recording and updating consent;
...
- Perform due diligence and periodic audits to confirm that third party providers are accurately maintaining customer databases and functional unsubscribe facilities;
...
- Ensure informative communications (e.g. regarding order confirmation and delivery updates) are not accompanied by links to the business’ website or other material that may be considered a CEM;
...
- Train customer-facing staff to ensure proper processes for obtaining and recording consent; and
...
- Monitor for common technical issues that may lead to contraventions, including non-functioning unsubscribe facilities, changes to the message a customer is required to send to unsubscribe (e.g. from ‘stop’ to ‘stopnow’) and inadvertent duplication of customer records.
...
One thing is clear, Australian businesses cannot afford to be complacent about Spam Act compliance. ACMA is becoming increasingly active with enforcement action and the penalties and other sanctions such as the appointment of independent monitors and regular reporting to ACMA can be costly to business. So can the damage to a business’ reputation, which can be substantial.

...
This Statistical Bulletin presents first results on enrolments in mainstream primary and post primary schools on 30th September 2025. The data is preliminary in nature; final data will be published at the end of the school year in June 2026. Please note that enrolment data includes enrolments of Ukrainian children. Further data on Ukrainian enrolments as of December 2025 can be found in the appendix to this document.
...
The source for this data is the Annual Census for 2025/26, which is returned via the Primary/Post-Primary Online Database (POD/P-POD). The primary level data reports enrolments in mainstream schools only. Data is anchored on the census date of 30th September 2025. Note that only schools aided by the Department of Education are included in this report.
...
This data is provisional and was published in February 2026. Final data will be published in June 2026. The final data will replace the provisional data.
...
In September 2025, the beginning of the 2025/26 school year, total enrolments in mainstream primary schools stood at 535,620 pupils, a decrease of 6,759, or 1.2%, on September 2024 (542,379). The number of girls decreased by 3,422 pupils, from 265,218 to 261,796, and the number of boys decreased by 3,337 from 277,161 to 273,824.
...
While enrolments in primary schools had been falling since 2018, the recent increase beginning in 2022 was driven by Ukrainian pupils. Ukrainian student enrolments stood at 10,166 in September 2025, a decrease of 152 since September 2024. Excluding Ukrainian pupils, mainstream school enrolments stood at 525,454 in September 2025, a fall of 6,645 from 2024.

##### Why does the $79 plan offer more features than the $1000 plan?
...
Because we know that no one wants to pay for stuff they don't need. Some of our most valued customers are able to reach their fundraising goals during a single "Big Night" annual event. These are typically established traditional auctions which reliably bring in over $50k. Our $1000 plan was designed for groups like these - that need only our most traditional tools and have enough confidence in their fundraising forecast to know they'll save money with the fixed price plan.
...
On the other hand, if your group is new to fundraising - or has modest goals - the Acorn plan is an affordable way to access full-service software. So why does the $79 plan offer more features? Because having a bigger toolbox will help your organization reach your goal more easily - and when you succeed, we succeed.

Title: Auctria Costs
URL: https://academy.auctria.com/getting_started/auctria_costs/
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
Auctria is designed to be flexible and affordable for events of all sizes. This page gives a quick overview of costs you might encounter while using Auctria, including licensing, credit card processing, text messaging credits, and optional services.
...
## License Pricing
...
Auctria licenses are based on a 12-month period and include unlimited events during that time. Your plan tier is determined by the total income from all events held during the license period.
...
| License Tier | Price | Annual Income Limit | Example Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Explorer | `FREE` | Up to $10,000 | Try out the platform |
| Emerald | `$375/yr` | Up to $50,000 | Small-to-mid fundraisers |
| Diamond | `$750/yr` | Unlimited | Large-scale fundraising events |
...
To accept online payments through Auctria — for donations, ticket sales, auction purchases, or sponsorships — you’ll need to connect a payment processor. Auctria does not process or hold any funds directly.
...
Stripe is directly integrated with Auctria and is the fastest and easiest way to start accepting payments. Payments are securely processed and deposited into your Stripe account. Auctria charges a small platform fee based on your license tier.
...
| Plan | Auctria Fee | Processor Fee (Stripe) | Total Fees |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Explorer | `1.00%` | `~2.9%` + `$0.30` per transaction | `$0.30` + `3.9%` per transaction |
| Emerald | `0.50%` | `~2.9%` + `$0.30` per transaction | `$0.30` + `3.4%` per transaction |
| Diamond | `0.25%` | `~2.9%` + `$0.30` per transaction | `$0.30` + `3.15%` per transaction |
...
- Included Credits: Emerald licenses include `1000` initial credits and Diamond licenses include `3000` initial credits.
- Additional Credits: Available in bundles of `1000` for `$25`
- Usage: Each message (sent or received) uses 1 credit
...
Prefer expert guidance? Auctria Launch services provide hands-on setup so you can focus on fundraising while we take care of the details.
...
- Launch Foundation is ideal for self-managed events that want professional setup, website configuration, and reliable event-night backup.
- Launch Advantage adds limited guest, ticket, and seating support—perfect for mid-sized events up to 250 guests.
- Launch Premier is a fully customized experience for large or complex events that need advanced ticket management and personalized support.
...
| Feature | Launch Foundation | Launch Advantage | Launch Premier |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Starting Price | $499/event | $749/event | Contact Us (from $749) |
| Launch Calls | 3 calls | 5 calls | Customized |
| Event Website Setup | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Ticket, Sponsorship & Raffle Setup | Items added & listed for sale | ✅ | ✅ |
| Ticket & Sponsorship Management | — | Up to 250 guests | 250+ guests |
| • Guest email support & ticket triggering | — | ✅ | ✅ |
| • Direct purchaser follow-up | — | — | ✅ |
| Auction Item Import | 1 import (8-hr turnaround during business hours) | 1 import (4-hr turnaround during business hours) | Customized |
| • Additional imports | $50 each | $50 each | Customized |
| Seating / Table Support | — | Up to 250 guests | 250+ guests |
| Event-Night Phone Support | 6-hour emergency window | 6-hour emergency window | ✅ |

143:    Differentiation still scores Aucly 2, correctly, because the wedge is
144:    contested — that is not overweighting, it is the honest reading.
145: 9. **Does it underweight ease/cost of building and testing?** No:
146:    validation_speed_cost and feasibility both score 4 here; the scorecard
147:    rewards cheap falsifiability. Pre-launch it was the founder's sequencing, not
148:    the scorecard, that skipped the cheap test.
149: 10. **Distinguishes viable small business from venture-scale?** Yes. No
150:     dimension requires venture scale; small size shows up in economics,
151:     distribution, differentiation and risk without auto-killing, and the
152:     threshold tests evidence quality, not ambition.
153: 11. **Does it recognise payment behaviour without over-reading ~7 purchases?**
154:     Yes: `evidence_strength` rose to 4 and `buyer_budget_clarity` stayed at 3,
155:     while `distribution` (2), `economics` (2) and `differentiation` (2) were not
156:     inflated. A handful of payments cannot lift retention, market size or
157:     channel scores, because none of those are evidenced.
158: 12. **Dimensions where current evidence still does not justify a strong
159:     score?** distribution (negative evidence), differentiation (contested),
160:     economics (unquantified), buyer (payment count unverified), founder_fit
161:     (time economics unknown), problem (no incumbent-dissatisfaction evidence).
162: 
163: ### Comparison with existing fixtures
164: 
165: | Idea | State | Score | Evidence level | Why this outcome |
166: |---|---|---|---|---|
167: | Aucly | parked | 60.0 | Commercial (early) | Real payments and real auctions, but unpaid distribution, retention and economics unproven; below threshold and no fail |
168: | GrantScout | killed | 55.8 | Plausible | No real-world evidence; veto on `defensible_wedge` (free GOV.UK discovery + GovOwed) |
169: | GeoNerd | parked | 49.5 | Promising | Genuine category discontinuity but all desk research; wedge contested by incumbents |
170: | ShiftSwap | killed | 44.2 | Plausible | Fails distribution, network-effect and margin filters; commodity feature bundled in rota software |
171: | WonkyBox | killed | 36.8 | Plausible | Oddbox loss-making at scale; paid acquisition required; margins fail |
172: 
173: The ordering is sensible: demonstrated payment behaviour (Aucly) outranks new-
174: category desk research (GeoNerd), which outranks ideas killed on hard filters or
175: hostile economics. Aucly is not advanced merely for having launched: it remains
176: below the threshold exactly because launch revealed distribution weakness rather
177: than validating it. GrantScout scoring above GeoNerd while being killed is also
178: consistent — its kill is a hard-filter veto, not an aggregate score.
179: 
180: ### Apparent false positive / negative or scoring anomaly
181: 
182: - **Pre-launch false negative:** none — the lab would have tested, not killed.
183: - **False positive:** none — the lab would not have advanced it to
184:   `validation-ready` (49.5), so it never claimed more than a hypothesis.
185: - **Scoring anomaly found (systematic):** the v1.1.0 missing-why-now cap applied
186:   at every evidence level, double-penalising evergreen businesses once real
187:   commercial evidence existed (Aucly's `problem_severity_frequency` was capped at
188:   2, worth ~3 points of total). Fixed in v1.2.0 by scoping the cap to
189:   `Plausible`/`Promising`.
190: - **No change needed** for: hard-filter pass/unknown/fail semantics; treatment
191:   of direct competitors; treatment of small/niche markets; weighting of cheap
192:   build/testability; founder fit; evidence strength; willingness-to-pay
193:   evidence; retention handling; distribution difficulty; bootstrapped vs
194:   venture-scale distinction.
195: 
196: ## Method refinement (v1.2.0)
197: 
198: - **Specific result exposing the problem:** Aucly today scored
199:   `problem_severity_frequency` 2 under the v1.1.0 cap (total 57.0) despite real
200:   auctions, real bidders and paying organisers.
201: - **Why the old rule was systematically wrong:** "no recent discontinuity" was
202:   being treated as evidence of weak demand. Evidence levels already distinguish
203:   pre-demand from demand/commercial evidence, so the cap should bind only where
204:   no demand evidence exists.
205: - **Change:** the missing/unevidenced why-now cap now applies only to ideas at
206:   `Plausible` or `Promising`; at `Demand evidence` or better the idea is judged
207:   on its operating evidence.
208: - **Regression check:** the killed fixtures (ShiftSwap, WonkyBox, GrantScout) are
209:   all `Plausible`, so the cap still applies and their kills rest on `fail`
210:   filters/vetoes; GeoNerd and Reasonable Steps (`Promising`) are unaffected;
211:   Aucly's change is a single dimension, 2→3.
212: - **Falsification preserved:** threshold unchanged at 65; hard filters
213:   unchanged; no weak idea becomes a pass.
214: - **Review:** method 1.2.0 change is `requested` —
215:   `reviews/2026-09-21-method-v1.2.0-review-request.md`; outcome to be recorded in
216:   `method/CHANGELOG.md` and answered next run.
217: 
218: ## Reasons if killed
219: 
220: Not killed. A kill would require evidence that organisers will not switch or pay
221: (for example 0 of 20 launches in the channel test with incumbent-satisfaction
222: objections). A killed variant would keep this record and could produce a
223: non-inheriting seed (e.g. purpose-built tools for volunteer-run charity auctions
224: in other verticals).
225: 
226: ## False-negative audit
227: 
228: Not applicable — Aucly has never been killed.
229: 
230: ## Decision log
231: 
232: | Date | Change | Reason | Actor |
233: |---|---|---|---|
234: | 2026-09-21 | Added; scored 60.0; parked at `adversarially-researched`; experiment `aucly-channel-test` proposed | Issue #3 calibration: recognise early commercial evidence without over-claiming; name remaining unknowns in a cheap pre-fixed test | worker |

      "summary": "## Research batches 4–7: regulation, tax, privacy, market size, incumbents (locale expansion of `aucly`)\n\nAll sources dated as noted; use as cited evidence in the two new `evidence/aucly/2026-09-22-*` files and in `ideas/aucly/expansion-assessment.md`.\n\n### Tax / indirect tax\n- **New Zealand GST on remote services** (IRD, \"Supplying remote services into New Zealand\", page dated 2026-09-12; IR546 2026 guide; IS 21/03): a non-resident business supplying remote services from outside NZ to NZ-resident customers must register/collect/return GST when total supplies to NZ customers were **NZ$60,000+ in the last 12 months or expected in the next 12 months**. No registration needed if it only supplies remote services to NZ GST-registered businesses for business use (those supplies are treated as outside NZ / zero-rated). NZ has a non-resident business claimant registration (s 54B) for input-tax recovery.\n- **EU/Ireland VAT – One Stop Shop** (European Commission pages vat-one-stop-shop.ec.europa.eu: \"The One Stop Shop\", \"VAT One Stop Shop\", \"Register to OSS\", \"Guide to the VAT One Stop Shop\"; corroborated by OpenAccountants \"EU OSS Digital\" skill, validation date April 2026). Key points: annual **EUR 10,000** threshold for cross-border B2C TBE (telecommunications, broadcasting, electronic) services — but the threshold benefit requires the supplier to be established in **only one Member State** (or, absent establishment, have permanent address/usual residence there). **Non-EU-established businesses cannot use the Union scheme to declare services; they must use the Non-Union OSS or register in each Member State, and must always charge the destination-country rate (no threshold benefit).** Ireland standard VAT 23%. Two pieces of non-contradictory evidence needed for consumer location (billing address default below €100k); retain records 10 years. Practical implication: a UK (non-EU) seller reaching Irish consumers must charge Irish VAT from the first sale and file via Non-Union OSS or per-state registration.\n- **US sales tax / economic nexus** (Wolters Kluwer \"Economic nexus simplified: State sales tax guide\" 2025-10-07; Avalara economic-nexus guide; TaxCloud \"Sales Tax Nexus by State Chart 2026\" 2026-01-26; nexusbystate.com economic-nexus map checked 2026-08-10; salestaxapplication.net reviewed 2026-08-18; Beancount.io 2026-07-22). Post-Wayfair every sales-tax state has an economic-nexus rule. **41 states use $100,000**; Alabama and Mississippi $250,000; California, New York and Texas $500,000; **New York requires BOTH >$500,000 sales AND >100 transactions**; ~16 states retain a transaction-count alternative; Illinois repealed its transaction test effective 2026-01-01; Alaska repealed 2025, Utah 2025. SaaS/digital products count as taxable in many states (e.g. NY treats SaaS as tangible personal property; Maryland taxes software/digital goods). Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon have no statewide sales tax. Charitable exemptions vary. Threshold is per state; marketplace-facilitated sales may or may not count. Implication: selling SaaS to US customers can trigger multi-state registration/filing once thresholds are crossed (and physical-presence nexus exists separately).\n- **Australia GST on imported services** (ATO pages dated 2025-09-11; ATO GSTR 2017/1): non-resident suppliers of imported services/digital products to Australian consumers must register for GST if GST turnover from sales connected with Australia is **A$75,000+** (A$150,000 for non-profit organisations); 10% GST; supplies to GST-registered business recipients are excluded; simplified GST registration available without an ABN.\n\n### Data protection / privacy\n- **EU GDPR Article 27 (European representative)** (LexisNexis practical guidance page updated 2026-05-26; BCLP article 2021-06-21; ICO \"Receiving personal information from the EEA\" page dated 2026-01-15; Taylor Wessing 2020-10-30; Robert Melton 2026-05-16). A UK-based controller with no EEA establishment that offers goods/services to, or monitors, individuals in the EEA must **appoint an EU/EEA representative in writing**, located in a Member State where affected data subjects are. Appointment does not transfer liability; it is a local contact point for supervisory authorities/data subjects, identity must be disclosed (Arts 13/14). Post-Brexit the UK GDPR has a parallel UK-representative duty; an EU representative does **not** satisfy the UK requirement and vice versa. There has been at least one EU fine for failure to appoint. The ICO confirms UK organisations comply with EU GDPR when targeting EEA individuals and need an EEA representative.\n- **Australia Privacy Act 1988 – small business exemption** (OAIC \"Small business\" page; 4it.com.au \"Has the Privacy Act small business exemption been removed?\" Sept 2026; Dentons 2026-09-03; Aitken 2026-09-02; Rules Mate 2026-05-18; AGD exposure draft Privacy Amendment (Personal Data Protection) Bill 2026, released 2026-08-31, submissions closed 2026-09-18). Section 6D exemption for businesses with annual turnover **A$3 million or less remains in force as at September 2026**; the tranche-2 exposure draft does **not** remove it (nor the employee-records exemption). Carve-outs apply regardless of turnover (health service providers holding health info, trading in personal information, Commonwealth contractors, credit reporting, TFN recipients, AML/CTF designated services from 2026-07-01, CDR-accredited, opted-in). ADM transparency and the Children's Online Privacy Code commence 2026-12-10; penalties up to A$50m/3× benefit/30% adjusted turnover for serious or repeated breaches. Removal of the small-business exemption is recommended/in-principle-agreed but not law and has no commencement date.\n- **New Zealand Privacy Act 2020** (legislation.govt.nz Privacy Act 2020 No 31, as at 2025-11-27, s 8 meaning of \"NZ agency\"; securitypolicy.com.au guide; Sprintlaw NZ 2026-07-07; compliancekit.co 2026-04-26; bdemerson.com). Applies to almost every organisation (\"agency\") **regardless of size** — **no turnover-based small-business exemption** (unlike Australia). Covers businesses, sole traders, not-for-profits, clubs and charities; can cover **overseas agencies carrying on business in New Zealand including through online activity**. Every agency must appoint a privacy officer. 13 Information Privacy Principles; notifiable privacy breach scheme; OPC is the regulator. IPP 12/13 deal with cross-border disclosure. Practically: Aucly serving NZ users would be an overseas agency carrying on business in NZ and must comply with no de minimis.\n\n### Fundraising / charity / gaming regulation\n- **Ireland** (Charities Regulator \"Guidelines for Charitable Organisations on Fundraising from the Public\", issued 2017-09-28 under s 14(1)(i) Charities Act 2009; Charities Act 2009 s 97; The Wheel summary 2026-03-24; Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland \"Charitable/Philanthropic Licences\"). Charities Regulator is the statutory regulator since Oct 2014; guidelines apply to all public fundraising including via third-party agents, which need written contracts specifying costs and the percentage reaching the charitable purpose. Data protection section points to the Data Protection Commissioner's charity-sector guidance and to direct/interactive marketing rules (direct mail, email, telemarketing, digital/social, SMS). Trustees must keep proper books and report annually; must be able to give a full financial account of each fundraising event (gross raised, costs, allocation). Gambling Regulation Act 2024: the GRAI may issue a gambling licence for charitable/philanthropic purposes covering relevant games, pool betting and **relevant lotteries**; certain charitable lotteries are exempt; the charitable/philanthropic licence type is **not expected to open for applications in 2026**, so charities continue under the current permit system. (Auctions are a sale mechanism, not a lottery; raffles/lotteries are the gambling-licensed activity.)\n- **United States charitable solicitation** (IRS \"Charitable solicitation – state requirements\" page last reviewed 2026-06-28; Colorado Secretary of State \"Charities and Fundraisers FAQs\"; LegalClarity \"Charitable Solicitation Laws\" 2026-05-14 and \"Are Silent Auctions Legal?\" 2026-08-06; 501c3.org \"Understanding Charitable Solicitations Registration\"; charitylawyerblog.com 2022-04-04). **~41 states + DC require charitable organisations to register with a state agency before soliciting residents**; fees commonly $25–$300, annual renewals, late penalties, suspension of the right to solicit, and per-violation civil penalties ($1,000–$5,000 common) with criminal exposure in some states. Registration is the organising charity's duty, in each state where it solicits, including online. The **Charleston Principles** (NASCO, 2001, non-binding) treat an interactive website as triggering registration where the charity specifically targets a state's residents or receives repeated/substantial contributions from that state; some states treat a passive donate button as a trigger. **A live or silent auction to raise funds is considered a solicitation for contributions** (Colorado FAQ explicitly: a charity silent auction requires charity registration, not a Bingo-Raffle licence; from 2026-08-12 Colorado auctioneers providing services to a charity are exempt from \"paid solicitor\" registration if they do not receive/handle contributions). Online auctions add solicitation exposure in states where the organisation is not registered. The **Unified Registration Statement** is accepted by 36+ jurisdictions; fees typically $25–$300.\n- **Australia anti-spam** (Spam Act 2003 (Cth) - Federal Register of Legislation; ACMA enforcement; Sprintlaw Australia guide 2025-06-16; Norton Rose Fulbright commentary). Commercial electronic messages need consent (express or reasonably inferred), clear sender identification, and a functional unsubscribe processed within 5 business days; charities have a consent exemption in some contexts as \"designated senders\" but identification and unsubscribe still apply. ACMA penalties scale per message/day; enforcement rising (e.g. DoorDash >$2m infringement).\n\n### Market size (updated) and incumbents (updated)\n- **Ireland primary schools: 3,067 mainstream primary schools** in 2025/26 with **535,620 pupils**, avg 174.6/school, down 1.2% year on year (Department of Education and Youth, \"Preliminary Statistical Bulletin 2025/26\" — census 30 Sep 2025, published Feb 2026, final data June 2026; schoolnumbers.ie; CSO ED106 dataset last updated 2026-09-21). Combined with the 721 post-primary schools already recorded, Ireland has roughly **3,788 schools** total, a small market.\n- **SchoolAuction.net pricing** (schoolauction.net/pricing and resources/buyers-guide/event-fit-cost, 2025-01-29). US-focused, designed for schools/PTAs/small community nonprofits, requires a valid 501(c)(3) (Acorn/Essentials require a US business or non-profit tax id). Plans: **Acorn $79/event + 3% performance fee + 3% + $0.30 card** (pay-as-you-grow); **Essentials $1,000/yr** (no performance fee, 3% + $0.30 card); **Plus $1,500/yr** (unlimited event sites, mobile bidding, use own processor); **Professional $2,000/yr** (virtual live auctions, hybrid, personal support). Free trial. Supports in-person gala, online silent auction and hybrid.\n- **Auctria pricing** (auctria.com/pricing; academy.auctria.com getting_started/auctria_costs; auctria.com/blog/plan-update; Software Finder 2026-05-06). **Explorer free** (up to $10,000 event income/year, 250 bidders, 1% Auctria card fee); **Emerald $375/yr** (up to $50,000 income, 750 bidders, 0.5% fee); **Diamond $750/yr** (unlimited income, 1,000 bidders, 0.25% fee). **No performance fees, ever**; no annual % of proceeds. Optional paid Launch setup $499–$749/event and Assist sessions. Prices in USD for all customers except Canadians (CAD + HST). Stripe integrated; Auctria does not hold funds.\n- (From earlier batches, retained: GalaBid — Sydney origin, ~1,000 events/year across AU & NZ, free plan funded by optional tips, Pro 4.9%, flat US$1,250/campaign, region-specific pricing; Region-specific incumbents: Australia — AirAuctioneer, Oktion; New Zealand — **Toko (toko.co.nz, Auckland) is 100% free for NZ schools, 5% for associations**, Windcave payments, claims to be the only NZ-specialised service, and Raised (raised.nz) free for cash/bank transfer with Stripe card fees paid by supporters; Ireland — iDonate.ie (5,000+ causes, online raffles, low fees), Fundraising Solutions (fundraisingsolutions.co, zero platform fee, \"fully compliant with Irish fundraising guidelines\"), FundRaisely.ie (payment tracking/reconciliation), eBay Ireland charity auctions; US — SchoolAuction.net, Auctria, GalaBid, plus other US gala platforms.)\n\n### Run metadata / files (from the same message)\n- **Run id generated: `20260922T100404Z`** (UTC, Tue 22 Sep 2026 10:04:04 UTC). Use `20260922T100404Z-normal` as the run directory and summary path.\n- Existing `evidence/aucly/` files (all dated 2026-09-21): `2026-09-21-pricing-and-payments.md`, `2026-09-21-live-auctions-and-customers.md`, `2026-09-21-competitive-landscape.md`, `2026-09-21-build-and-operating-burden.md`, `2026-09-21-seo-and-acquisition.md` (no evidence index file present).\n- Existing `ideas/aucly/` files: `scorecard.json`, `pre-launch-assessment.md`, `decision.md`, `dossier.md`.\n\nWeb-lookup budget used so far in this run: approximately 25 of the 40 allowed (all research above, plus earlier batches); remaining headroom ~15."

81: commission tail. Roughly seven paid auctions are owner-supplied and unverified
82: (no lifetime export found). Hosting (Railway, Postgres/Redis), email (Brevo) and
83: a continuing founder maintenance burden are real costs; per-auction contribution
84: is not quantified. Modelled-only economics cap the score at 2.
85: 
86: ## Founder fit
87: 
88: The founder built and continues to operate the product, shipping a broad feature
89: set and handling real customer workflows — evidenced execution fit. Domain
90: access, sales capacity and founder-time economics are not evidenced. Score 3.
91: 
92: ## Strongest supporting case
93: 
94: Real organisers used the platform for real events: Furzedown Primary PTA
95: auctioned 44 lots to 63 unique bidders, taking 1,074 bids and raising £2,265,
96: and a Lingfield Foundation golf-day auction raised £2,500 with a positive
97: organiser quote. Active auctions appear in first-party analytics. The category
98: demonstrably moves money (competitors charge commission or fees; PTA Events
99: reports £40m processed). The build and payment plumbing are done, and the
100: £0/£60/£120 flat-fee offer is simple and priced below typical incumbents'
101: commission on a £2,000+ auction.
102: 
103: ## Adversarial case (strongest case this is wrong)
104: 
105: Distribution is failing in the one channel that has been measured: after
106: substantial SEO work, a recorded window of 2,333 visitors produced zero
107: accounts, zero launches and zero revenue, and commercial queries have zero
108: clicks. The category is occupied by entrenched providers with network effects
109: and reputation, and free plans blunt the flat-fee wedge. The economics are
110: structurally small — one-off £60/£120 per event with no commission tail and a
111: heavy maintenance burden — and neither retention, market size nor founder-time
112: contribution is evidenced. On this evidence Aucly could be a technically
113: excellent, well-loved small project that never becomes a worthwhile business,
114: and the honest reading of the ~7 paid auctions is early evidence, not
115: validation.
116: 
117: ## Unresolved assumptions
118: 
119: | Ref | Assumption | Status 2026-09-21 | Resolve via |
120: |---|---|---|---|
121: | A1 | Organisers feel enough pain with incumbents to switch | Unknown | win/loss questions in the channel test |
122: | A2 | Flat fee is more attractive than commission to this buyer | Unknown | price-model reaction in the channel test |
123: | A3 | Organisers can be reached without paid acquisition | Negative so far (0 accounts from 2,333 visitors) | aucly-channel-test |
124: | A4 | A volunteer can self-serve an auction with low support | Partially evidenced (Furzedown, Lingfield ran with limited help) | support load recorded per launch |
125: | A5 | £60/£120 per auction yields workable contribution | Unknown | hosting/email cost + founder hours per auction |
126: | A6 | Organisers return in a second year | Unknown | retention follow-up after experiment |
127: | A7 | Enough UK PTAs/schools/charities run auctions | Unknown | market sizing from public data; incumbent scale |
128: 
129: ## Cheapest decisive experiment
130: 
131: `aucly-channel-test` (proposed, awaiting human approval): approach 20 UK PTAs
132: outside the founder's network through organisational contact addresses, with the
133: Furzedown case study and free setup help; proceed only if at least 2 launch a
134: real auction within 30 days at zero paid spend. Cost bound: ~20 human hours,
135: £0, 30 days. It tests the central assumption (unpaid distribution) and gives
136: win/loss input on the wedge.
137: 
138: ## Decision log
139: 
140: | Date | Change | Reason | Actor |
141: |---|---|---|---|
142: | 2025-07-30 | Build started (outside the lab) | No recorded screening artefact; recorded here for calibration | founder (historical) |
143: | 2026-09-21 | Added to ledger as calibration case; scored 60.0; parked at `adversarially-researched`; experiment proposed | Issue #3: early commercial evidence but unproven sustainability; below threshold 65; remaining unknowns named in the proposed experiment | worker |

(End of file - total 143 lines)

## Bottom line: don't expand now

The binding constraint on Aucly is **distribution at home**, not geography. The recorded first-party data shows 2,333 visitors → 0 accounts, 0 auctions launched, £0 revenue from the SEO/acquisition channel, and the closest-to-validation-ready experiment is still unapproved. Expanding resets distribution to zero in markets where the price competition is *equal or stronger*.

## What the four locales actually look like

| Locale | Schools | Entry-level incumbent | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ireland** | ~3,788 (3,067 primary, 721 post-primary) | Fundraising Solutions (0% platform fee); iDonate.ie | Best cheap probe, weakest standalone; worst early VAT (UK non-EU seller must charge Irish 23% from first sale) |
| **Australia** | 9,673 | GalaBid (~1,000 events/yr AU+NZ); free-with-tips | Real market, but entrenched incumbent + timezone support cost |
| **New Zealand** | 2,536 | **Toko is 100% free for NZ schools**; Raised.nz | Smallest; free incumbent; Privacy Act 2020 has no small-business exemption |
| **United States** | ~99,300 public | Auctria free tier; SchoolAuction.net from $79/event; GalaBid | Largest, but saturated at *both* price ends; multi-state sales tax + 41-state solicitation patchwork |

**Cost:** localisation (currency, domain, email deliverability, timezone support) is the cheap part; the dominant cost is founder time/opportunity cost. **Benefit (modelled, not evidence):** UK at 5% penetration (~£147k/yr) exceeds Ireland + NZ + Australia at 1% combined (~£19k/yr) — i.e. geography is not the bottleneck.

**Regulation/tax** (two cited evidence files): indirect tax only bites once money moves (a free-tier probe avoids it), NZ GST above NZ$60k, AU GST above A$75k, Irish VAT from the first sale, US multi-state nexus at ~$100k/state; NZ Privacy Act has no de minimis, AU still has the A$3m exemption, GDPR Art. 27 EEA-representative needed if targeting Ireland.

## Recommendation

1. **Ireland first** *if* expansion is pursued — not because it's attractive standalone, but because it's the cheapest *discriminating* test: small, English-speaking, common-law, and you already know the VAT worst case.
2. Approve **`aucly-channel-test`** (UK, £0, ~20h) before any locale work — it's the gate for everything.
3. Then the conditional **`aucly-ireland-demand`** (20 Irish PTAs, ≥2 launch/30 days, £0, ~20h) that I proposed; its decision rule is explicitly keyed to the UK test outcome.

The question: make it a successful highly profitable business. I should be honest: "highly profitable" with a one-off £60/£120 price and a service-heavy, volunteer-buyer niche is hard; the current model caps out. So the strategy must change the economics, not just the geography.

Let me think about what actually drives profitability in this niche:
1. **Recurring revenue, not one-off.** One-off £60/£120 per auction means every year you re-acquire the customer. Profitable businesses in this niche either charge a % of proceeds (GalaBid 4.9%, Jumblebee 5%) or annual subscription (Auctria $375-750, SchoolAuction.net $1,000-2,000, Generosity Works £995). Flat-fee one-off is the worst of both: low price, no tail, high re-acquisition cost.
   - The wedge "no commission" is a real customer benefit (PTAs hate losing 5% of proceeds). But it should be captured as **annual subscription** (e.g. £99-£149/yr unlimited auctions) or a **flat fee per event that recurs** via an annual membership. That converts a one-off into an annuity and aligns with "no commission".
   - Actually the most profitable and defensible: **annual membership for the school/PTA** — one relationship, recurring auctions (summer fair, Christmas, quiz), plus other fundraising tools. This is what PTA Events does (broader PTA platform). Aucly's risk is being "a feature of a PTA suite" — so the counter is either be the best auction tool and partner/distribute through suites, or become the suite.

2. **Fix the channel first — this is the real bottleneck.** The single most important fact: 0 demonstrated unpaid channel. No amount of pricing/packaging fixes that. So step 1: run the channel test, and if direct outreach works, systematise it (partnerships with PTA federations, county PTA associations, school business manager networks, charity infrastructure bodies, MSE-style content, Facebook PTA groups). If it doesn't work unpaid, the business needs a paid channel with LTV > CAC — which the one-off model cannot support. So channel and pricing are linked: **recurring revenue is what makes paid acquisition viable.**

3. **Narrow the ICP.** "Schools, PTAs and small charities" is too broad. The proven case is a primary-school PTA with a 7-day online auction (Furzedown). Small charities have different needs (Gift Aid, raffles, compliance). Pick the segment where the product already wins and where repeat behaviour is highest: **primary-school PTAs / parent councils in the UK**, then expand to PTAs more broadly, then small charities.

4. **Productisation to cut service cost.** Volunteer buyers need hand-holding. If every auction needs founder setup, margins fail (plausible_margins unknown). So: templates, AI item description (already built), done-for-you import, checklist, a "launch in 30 minutes" flow, and a library of proven item catalogues. Reduce human hours per auction toward zero. This is where AI actually helps: generating lot descriptions, suggested starting bids/prices from comparable lots, reminder sequences, post-auction reconciliation.

5. **Monetise beyond the flat fee without breaking the "no commission" promise.** 
   - Payment processing: if Aucly becomes a payment facilitator (Stripe Connect) it can earn a spread or take a small platform fee, but that's commission-like and adds money-transmission risk (currently avoided — a deliberate strength: no funds held).
   - Value-added paid add-ons: printed catalogues, professional photography, buyer-email design, match-funding/Gift Aid handling, live-event screens/streaming, "auctioneer for the night" marketplace (Generosity Works' model), sponsorship packs.
   - Sponsor/brand marketplace: local businesses sponsor auctions; Aucly takes a placement fee. This is a second-order money stream that doesn't touch the organiser's proceeds.
   - Data/benchmarking: "what lots raise most" reports — weak, probably not sellable.
   - SaaS to the adjacent buyer: churches, sports clubs, Rotary, museums, hospices — same product, bigger TAM.

6. **Geographic expansion is a later lever, not the first.** (Consistent with the assessment.) If UK channel works, Ireland/AU are cheap English-language copies; US needs a different playbook (charitable solicitation registration, state tax, entrenched free tiers).

With 20% net margin, that's ~£24k/yr profit — not "highly profitable" but a good lifestyle business. To get to £1m ARR you need ~8,000 members at £120 or ~2,000 at £500 (which requires the multi-tool suite or larger charities/events).
   - Path B: **Commission/percentage model** — higher revenue per event but loses the differentiator and competes head-on with GalaBid/Jumblebee on their turf; differentiation was already scored 2.
   - Path C: **Become the PTA platform** (auctions + raffles + ticketing + payments + Gift Aid), competing with PTA Events. Higher ceiling, much higher build/distribution cost, and PTA Events has a decade head start.
   - Path D: **Serve the professional fundraiser / charity gala market** (higher budgets, managed service, £995-£2,000/yr) — but that's a different, more competitive segment (Givergy, Generosity Works).
   - Honest conclusion: with the current one-off £60/£120 flat fee and no channel, it cannot be "highly profitable". The two changes that most increase expected value are (i) prove one repeatable unpaid channel and (ii) convert pricing to recurring/annual with value-adds. Everything else is secondary.

8. **What I'd do in the first 90 days (concrete).**
   - Week 0: instrument the funnel properly (bot-filtered analytics; event-level funnel: visit → account → auction created → launched → paid). You cannot manage what you can't measure.
   - Week 1-4: run `aucly-channel-test` (20 PTAs, ≥2 launches, £0). Simultaneously test a second channel: partnerships (county PTA associations / PTA UK / school business manager networks) and content/SEO done properly (target "how to run a school auction", "silent auction ideas", with a real tool CTA).
   - Week 3-6: run win/loss calls with the ~7 paying organisers and the non-converters: why did they choose Aucly? Would they have paid £120/yr? What would make them run again? Test price points: £60 one-off vs £120/yr membership vs 3% capped.
   - Week 6-10: instrument unit economics: founder hours per launch, hosting/email cost per auction, second-year return. This resolves `plausible_margins`.
   - Week 10-13: if ≥2 launches from a repeatable channel and organisers say yes to recurring, switch the model to annual membership with a free entry tier, and build the retention features (year-round fundraising, not just one auction).
   - If the channel test fails: the honest move is to **kill or park** — a business with no repeatable acquisition and a £120 ceiling is not highly profitable.

9. **Defensibility / moat.** The moat isn't the software (commoditised). It's: (a) a repeatable, low-cost channel (e.g. owning the "school auction" search intent + PTA-network partnerships), (b) switching costs from year-round usage and accumulated lot/catalogue data, (c) a two-sided local sponsor marketplace. Realistically, a niche tool can be copied; the defensible asset is distribution relationships and brand within the PTA community.

10. **Risks that could kill it:** volunteer buyer churn (new committee each year), seasonality, price sensitivity, incumbents bundling auctions free (PTA Events, GalaBid free tier), platform dependence (Stripe), and the founder's time becoming the hidden cost.

Aucly already has "Collect Payments". A payments-first product (card links, reconciliation, match funding/Gift Aid) could be monetised per transaction and recur. Good question — and the honest answer starts with a diagnosis, because the evidence says the product isn't the problem.

## The diagnosis

Aucly has a real product with real users (Furzedown: 44 lots, 63 bidders, 1,074 bids, £2,265). What it does **not** have is a business model. Two things are broken:

1. **No repeatable acquisition channel.** The only measured channel (SEO) is now known to be bot-contaminated and effectively untested; the ~7 paid auctions almost certainly came from your network. A business that can only acquire customers through the founder's contacts isn't a business yet.
2. **One-off pricing with no recurring revenue.** £60/£120 per auction means you re-acquire the same PTA every single year, and the price is too low to fund that. Every serious incumbent either takes a percentage (GalaBid 4.9%, Jumblebee 5%) or charges annually (Auctria $375–750, SchoolAuction.net $1,000–2,000, Generosity Works £995). One-off flat fee is the worst of both worlds: low price, no tail, high re-acquisition cost.

So: **I would not touch geography, and I would not add features, until those two are fixed.** Here's what I'd actually do.

## 1. Fix measurement first (days, not weeks)
The acquisition endpoint counts bots. I'd gate it on Cloudflare's bot score / exclude non-browser user agents server-side, and build an event-level funnel: visit → account → auction created → launched → paid. Right now you can't tell "SEO failing" from "conversion failing". That's the cheapest, highest-value fix in the whole business.

## 2. Prove one unpaid channel (the make-or-break)
Run the `aucly-channel-test` already proposed: 20 PTAs outside your network, case study + free setup, kill if 0 of 20 launch. In parallel, test the two channels a solo founder can actually scale:
- **Partnerships** — county PTA associations, PTA UK, school business manager networks, multi-academy trusts. One relationship reaches hundreds of PTAs. This is the most promising unpaid route and it's completely untested.
- **Intent-led content** — "how to run a school auction", "silent auction ideas", with the tool as the obvious answer, rather than generic blog posts.

If neither yields a repeatable conversation, the honest conclusion is that this needs a **paid** channel — and that only works if pricing changes (below). No channel = no business, regardless of everything else.

## 3. Change the model from one-off to annuity
Keep the "no commission" promise — it's your only real differentiator against GalaBid/Jumblebee — but capture it as **annual membership**, not a one-off event fee. Something like: free to try (15 items), then **£99–£149/year unlimited auctions** for the PTA, plus a higher tier for schools/charities running multiple events.

This transforms the economics:
- One relationship, recurring revenue, and retention becomes the growth engine instead of re-acquisition.
- It matches how PTAs actually behave — they fundraise year-round (summer fair, Christmas, quiz, sponsored events).
- It makes a paid channel viable, because LTV > CAC.

The test is cheap and decisive: ask the ~7 paying organisers and the non-converters whether they'd pay £120/year rather than £60 once. If they wouldn't, the model is wrong and you've learned it for the cost of a few calls.

## 4. Narrow the ICP
"Schools, PTAs and small charities" is three different businesses. The proven case is a **primary-school PTA running a 7-day online auction**. I'd own that segment completely, then extend to secondary schools and small charities only once retention is proven. Small charities need Gift Aid, raffles and compliance — a different product.

## 5. Drive service cost toward zero
`plausible_margins` is still unknown because nobody has measured founder hours per launch. Volunteer buyers need hand-holding, and if every auction needs you, margins fail. I'd measure it, then productise it away: proven lot-catalogue templates, AI item descriptions and suggested reserves, a "launch in 30 minutes" flow, automated payment chasing and reconciliation. You've already built the AI descriptions — push that advantage.

## 6. Add revenue that doesn't break the promise
- **Local sponsor marketplace** — businesses sponsor auctions; Aucly takes the placement fee. This doesn't touch the organiser's proceeds, so it's compatible with "no commission".
- **Paid add-ons** — printed catalogues, professional photography, live-event screens/streaming, an "auctioneer for the night" marketplace.
- **Payments/reconciliation as the wedge** — Furzedown tracked payments manually by bank transfer. Collecting money and chasing winners is the genuinely painful, recurring part. A payments-first product can be monetised per transaction and is stickier than the auction tool itself.

I'd **avoid** becoming a payments intermediary that holds funds — you currently don't, and that's a deliberate risk advantage.

## The honest economics
Illustratively (not evidence): 1,000 UK PTAs × £120/yr ≈ £120k ARR; at a realistic 20–25% net margin that's a good ~£25–30k/yr lifestyle business, not "highly profitable". To reach £1m ARR you need either ~8,000 members at £120, or ~2,000 at £500 — which means the multi-event/multi-tool or larger-charity segment. There is no version of a one-off £60 auction fee that gets there.

**So "highly profitable" requires picking a bigger ceiling:** either become the year-round PTA fundraising platform (competing with PTA Events, who have a decade's head start), or serve larger charity galas at £1,000–2,000/yr (competing with Givergy and Generosity Works). I'd only attempt the first after retention is proven on the narrow PTA wedge.

## What I'd refuse to do
- **Not fight on commission.** Charging 5% loses the only wedge you have.
- **Not expand geography first.** Ireland is cheap *after* the UK channel works; the US needs a different playbook entirely (state solicitation, sales tax, entrenched free tiers).
- **Not build more features.** You have plenty; you lack distribution and retention.

## The 90-day version
1. Fix analytics (week 0).
2. Run the channel test + partnership outreach (weeks 1–4).
3. Win/loss calls with the ~7 organisers; test annual pricing (weeks 3–6).
4. Measure hours and cost per auction; second-year return (weeks 6–10).
5. If ≥2 launches from a repeatable channel **and** organisers accept recurring pricing → switch to annual membership and build retention. If not → kill or park it honestly.

**The one metric that decides everything:** can you get 2 of 20 PTAs to launch an auction through a channel that isn't your personal network? Until that's yes, nothing else — pricing, features, Ireland, the US — changes the answer.

Understood — no customer contact, and no new signup fields. That's actually the better path, because **your existing referrer capture is stronger evidence than anything a survey would give you.**

## What to pull (zero user-facing change)

You already store the referrer, so the attribution question is answerable from data on disk:

1. **Filter existing referrers for AI engines** — `chatgpt.com`, `chat.openai.com`, `openai.com`, `perplexity.ai`, `copilot.microsoft.com`, `gemini.google.com`, `claude.ai`, plus Google organic.
2. **Cross-reference each of the ~7 paid auctions** back to its originating referrer/session — that converts "we think it came from search/ChatGPT" into a cited first-party fact.
3. **Classify converting `direct/none` sessions** — some AI and dark-social traffic arrives with no referrer, so anything that converted from "direct" is a candidate.
4. **Note the landing page** for AI referrals — that tells you *which* content gets cited, which is the seed of the repeatable channel.

## The one invisible improvement

Persist the **first-touch referrer server-side** (cookie/session or a column on the account) so it survives from first visit through to signup and payment. No field, no prompt, no friction — the user never sees it. That's the whole measurement fix; the "how did you hear about us?" field I suggested earlier is now off the table.

**Caveat to record honestly:** referrers get stripped (privacy settings, in-app browsers, link previewers), so what you capture is a **floor**, not the full AI share. "Often ChatGPT" almost certainly understates it. That's fine for a directional read, but the lab should not score it as a complete measurement.

## What this does to the diagnosis

It flips the core problem. It isn't "there is no channel" — it's "there is a channel that is **already producing paying customers and is not instrumented**." That is a much better starting position, and it makes the earlier recommendation sharper:

- **Pricing/retention** stays the biggest lever (one-off £60/£120 has no tail).
- **Geography** stays out of scope.
- **`aucly-channel-test` should be reframed.** Cold outreach to 20 PTAs is now the *wrong* first test — it tests a channel you may not need. The right cheapest test is: *can the inbound search/AI channel be made repeatable?* — publish/optimise content designed to be cited, then measure AI referrals and launched auctions. Still £0 and no customer hassle, but it tests the channel that already works.
